title: The Leviathan and the Great Refractors
summary: An Irish earl built a telescope so huge that it hung between two castle-sized stone walls, and with it he saw that some faraway clouds in space are shaped like whirlpools. Meanwhile, a French mathematician found a brand-new planet using only pencil, paper and gravity. In America, giant lens telescopes rose on mountaintops, until lenses simply could not grow any bigger.

sections.heading: A Giant Grows in an Irish Castle
paragraphs: Picture a small town in the middle of Ireland in the early 1840s. Green fields, peat bogs, a river, and a grey stone castle. In the castle grounds, dozens of local men are building something nobody in the world has ever seen: a telescope tube as long as a city bus, made of wood held together with iron hoops, so wide that, according to a famous story, a church dean once walked through it holding an open umbrella. The town was called Parsonstown back then (today it is Birr), and the man in charge was William Parsons, the 3rd Earl of Rosse.

Lord Rosse, born in 1800, was a nobleman and member of Parliament, but at heart he was an engineer who loved machinery, metalwork and mathematics. When he inherited the family estate in 1841, he gained the money and land to try something enormous: the biggest light-collecting telescope on Earth, able to see deeper into the faint, misty patches of the night sky than anyone ever had. He aimed for a mirror 72 inches (about 1.83 meters) across, roughly the height of a grown man.

There was no factory anywhere that could make such a thing, so Rosse built his own. He trained workers from his estate, many of them farm laborers with no special schooling, to become metal casters, blacksmiths and mirror grinders. There were no glass mirrors yet for telescopes; instead the mirror had to be cast from speculum metal, a hard, shiny mix of mostly copper and tin. Speculum is brittle, a bit like a giant cookie made of metal. If it cools too fast, it cracks. If it cools unevenly, it warps.

Rosse had already learned a great deal by building an earlier reflector about 36 inches wide. For the 72-inch disk, his team melted metal in furnaces on the estate, poured it into a mold, and let the glowing disk cool slowly for weeks in a special oven. Not every casting worked, and it took several attempts to produce two good mirrors. Why two? Speculum tarnishes, and repolishing changes its shape and takes a long time, so one mirror could sit in the telescope while the other was being polished.

Each finished mirror was about 5 inches (13 cm) thick and weighed almost 3 tons, about as much as two cars. The wooden tube was around 54 feet (16.5 meters) long, and with the mirror inside it weighed about 12 tons. The design was Newtonian: light bounced off the big curved mirror at the bottom and back up to a small flat mirror near the top, which turned it sideways to the eyepiece. So the observer had to stand way up at the top end, on galleries high above the ground.

Something so heavy could not be swung around freely. Instead, Rosse built two huge stone walls, each several stories high, standing side by side in a north-south line, with the tube hanging in the gap between them. Its bottom end sat on a giant swivel joint. Chains and a winch raised or lowered it, and beams and gears let it swing a little east or west. So the telescope could follow an object for only about an hour as Earth's turning carried it past the gap between the walls. Observers had to wait for their target to drift into view, then work fast.

The telescope was first used in early 1845. People soon nicknamed it the Leviathan of Parsonstown, after a giant sea monster in the Bible. It was the largest telescope in the world from 1845 until 1917, when the 100-inch Hooker Telescope in California was finished. That is more than 70 years at the top!

The Leviathan was born at a hard moment. In 1845 a disease struck Ireland's potato crop, the main food of millions of poor families, and the Great Famine followed. About a million people died over the next several years and many more left the country. Lord Rosse turned much of his attention to helping people on his estate, and regular observing was delayed. While the Leviathan looked at the stars, the people around it were living through one of the saddest times in their country's history.

sections.heading: The Whirlpool in the Dark
paragraphs: Ever since telescopes were invented, astronomers had noticed small faint smudges in the sky that did not look like sharp points of starlight. They called them nebulae, from the Latin word for clouds or mist. In the 1700s the French comet hunter Charles Messier made a list of these fuzzy objects so he would not confuse them with comets. On 13 October 1773 he found one near the handle of the Big Dipper and listed it as number 51. Today we call it M51.

Through Messier's small telescope, M51 looked like a faint round glow. Through Herschel's larger instruments it looked a bit more detailed, but still like a ring or a blob. Then, in the spring of 1845, Lord Rosse pointed the Leviathan at it. With so much more light pouring into his eye, he could see something astonishing: the glow was not a plain blob at all. It had curving arms, wrapping around a bright center like water swirling down a drain, with a smaller companion glow at the end of one arm.

Rosse made a careful drawing of what he saw. His sketch of M51 is one of the most famous pictures in the history of astronomy, because it was the first time anyone had seen spiral structure in a nebula. Later observers nicknamed M51 the Whirlpool, and some even called it Rosse's Galaxy. Over the following years he and his assistants found spiral shapes in several other nebulae too, and Rosse suggested that their shapes must come from some kind of motion governed by the laws of physics, since a spiral looks like something that is spinning.

Here is the amazing part: nobody in 1845 knew what a spiral nebula actually was. A small swirl of gas inside our Milky Way, perhaps a new solar system being born? Or a whole separate collection of stars, unimaginably far away? There was no way yet to measure their distance, and the answer would take almost 80 more years, as we will see in Part 13. Today we know M51 is a galaxy about 31 million light-years away and roughly 77,000 light-years wide, not far from the size of our Milky Way. The light Rosse saw had left it long before there were any humans on Earth.

Lord Rosse made other famous drawings too. Even before the Leviathan was finished, he sketched a nebula in the constellation Taurus with his earlier 36-inch telescope. The drawing looked, to people at the time, a bit like a crab with legs, and the name stuck: we still call it the Crab Nebula. Rosse also claimed in 1845 that the great telescope broke the Orion Nebula up into separate stars. John Herschel, William Herschel's son, disagreed, and he was right to be doubtful; the Orion Nebula really is a cloud of glowing gas, as the next part of our story will show.

Using the Leviathan was hard work. Ireland's skies are cloudy and damp, so clear nights were precious, and the observer, high on wooden galleries in the cold, had to draw everything by hand because cameras could not yet capture faint nebulae. After the 3rd Earl died in 1867, his son, the 4th Earl, kept the telescope working. The astronomer J. L. E. Dreyer used it from 1874 to 1878 and later compiled the New General Catalogue, the NGC, a giant list of nebulae and star clusters whose numbers astronomers still use. Observations made at Birr with Lord Rosse's telescopes added more than 200 objects to it.

The Leviathan was used until about 1890. After the 4th Earl died in 1908 it was partly taken apart, and in 1914 one of its speculum mirrors went to the Science Museum in London. For decades only the stone walls and old tube remained, like the bones of a dinosaur. In the 1990s engineers rebuilt it from old drawings, finishing the structure in 1997 and adding a new aluminium mirror in 1999. Right next door, a modern radio telescope station called I-LOFAR, opened in 2017, now listens to the sky in a way Lord Rosse never imagined.

sections.heading: A Planet Found with Pencil and Paper
paragraphs: While Lord Rosse was building his giant, astronomers had a planet-sized mystery on their hands. In Part 9 we met William Herschel, who discovered Uranus in 1781. Once astronomers knew about Uranus, they went back and calculated exactly where it should be in the sky year after year, using Isaac Newton's law of gravity and the pull of the Sun, Jupiter and Saturn. But Uranus refused to behave. Sometimes it was a little ahead of where the math said it should be, and sometimes a little behind.

Two young mathematicians took up the challenge, without knowing about each other. In England, John Couch Adams, a student and then young fellow at Cambridge University, began working on the problem in the 1840s and by 1845 had an estimate of where the unknown planet might be. He tried to interest George Airy, the Astronomer Royal at Greenwich, but the search in England started slowly. When the Cambridge Observatory finally did look, under its director James Challis, it did not compare its observations quickly enough to notice the new planet.

In France, Urbain Le Verrier worked independently. Imagine working backwards from Uranus's small wobbles to the position of a planet nobody had ever seen, with no computer, only pages and pages of hand-written sums. Le Verrier did exactly that and published a predicted position in June 1846, then sent his detailed results, including an estimated mass and orbit, to someone he hoped would search quickly: Johann Gottfried Galle at the Berlin Observatory in Germany.

Galle received Le Verrier's letter on the morning of 23 September 1846. That same day he asked the observatory's director, Johann Franz Encke, for permission to search, and got it. That night Galle sat at the observatory's 9-inch refractor, a fine lens telescope made by the Munich workshop that Joseph von Fraunhofer, whom we met in Part 8, had made famous. A young student astronomer, Heinrich d'Arrest, eagerly asked to help.

d'Arrest had a clever idea: compare the sky with a brand-new, detailed star chart of exactly that area, called Hora XXI. Galle called out the stars he saw one by one, and d'Arrest checked each against the chart. Just after midnight, Galle described a faint star of about 8th magnitude. According to the famous account, d'Arrest exclaimed that that star was not on the map! It was the new planet, less than one degree, about two full-Moon widths, from Le Verrier's predicted spot. The next night they checked again: it had moved, just as a planet should.

The discovery was a sensation. For the first time, a planet had been found not by accident, as Uranus had been, but because mathematics said it must be there. It was one of the greatest triumphs of Newton's law of gravity. Le Verrier was hailed as the man who discovered a planet with the point of his pen.

Then came the quarrel. British astronomers, including Airy, pointed out that Adams had made a prediction earlier, and French scientists felt the British were trying to grab credit for a French discovery. The Royal Society gave its Copley Medal to Le Verrier in 1846 and to Adams in 1848. Adams himself graciously credited Le Verrier. Historians still discuss it: studies of old documents, including work by Nicholas Kollerstrom, suggest Adams's predictions were less certain than the traditional story said. Today most give the main credit to Le Verrier and Galle, while recognizing Adams's impressive independent work.

Even the name caused arguments. The French astronomer François Arago wanted to call the planet Le Verrier. Others objected, and in the end astronomers agreed on a name from mythology to match the other planets: Neptune, the Roman god of the sea, fitting for a deep blue world. Just 17 days after the planet's discovery, the English brewer and amateur astronomer William Lassell, observing with a homemade reflector, found its largest moon, Triton.

Neptune is about 4.5 billion kilometers from the Sun, about 30 times farther than Earth. One trip around the Sun takes it about 165 years, so it was only in 2011 that Neptune finished its first full orbit since its discovery. And here is a twist: Galileo had actually seen Neptune through his telescope in 1612 and 1613, while watching Jupiter's moons, but he thought it was just a faint background star. The telescope Galle used to find Neptune still exists and is on display at the Deutsches Museum in Munich.

sections.heading: Silver on Glass: Goodbye, Heavy Metal
paragraphs: The Leviathan showed both the power and the problem of metal mirrors. Speculum was heavy, it cracked easily while cooling, and it tarnished. Even freshly polished, it reflected only around two-thirds of the light hitting it, and less as it grew dull. Re-polishing meant grinding away a thin layer of the surface, which could ruin the mirror's exact curve, so it had to be reshaped and tested all over again.

The answer came from chemistry. In 1835 the German chemist Justus von Liebig found a way to make a thin, even coat of silver form on glass using a chemical reaction in a liquid bath. He improved the method in 1856, and soon it was used to make household mirrors better and more cheaply. Two clever opticians saw that this could change telescopes forever.

In 1856 and 1857, the German optician Carl August von Steinheil and the French physicist Léon Foucault each made telescope mirrors in a new way. First, they ground and polished a disk of glass into exactly the right curved shape. Then they coated just the front surface with an ultra-thin layer of silver, much thinner than a sheet of paper. The light bounced off the silver without ever going into the glass. These were the first optical-quality front-surface glass mirrors.

Why was this so much better? Glass is far lighter than speculum, so mirrors could grow bigger, and it can be polished to a more accurate shape that it holds well. Fresh silver reflects much more light than speculum, so the same size mirror shows fainter things. Best of all, when the silver tarnished, you simply removed it with chemicals and put on a new coat, without touching the precious curved glass.

Foucault is also famous for hanging a long pendulum in the Panthéon in Paris in 1851, whose slowly turning swing showed that Earth spins. For telescopes, his key gift came in 1858: a simple way to test a mirror's shape. You shine a tiny point of light at the mirror and, where its reflection focuses, slide a knife edge across the beam while looking at the mirror. A perfect mirror darkens evenly; bumps and dips show up as light and shadow, like a landscape lit at sunset. Before this, mirror testing was largely trial and error. Mirror makers still use versions of the Foucault test, and the basic idea of a glass mirror with a whisper-thin metal skin (today usually aluminium, a method John Strong developed around 1930) is used in almost every big telescope.

sections.heading: The Painter Who Became a Lens Maker
paragraphs: While mirrors were improving in Europe, the best big lenses of the late 1800s came from a surprising place: a workshop in Cambridgeport, Massachusetts, run by a former portrait painter. Alvan Clark, born in 1804 in Ashfield, Massachusetts, earned his living painting portraits and making engravings, but he was deeply curious about telescopes. By about age 40 he had taught himself to grind and polish lenses, and he turned out to have an extraordinary gift for it. With his sons Alvan Graham Clark and George Bassett Clark he founded the firm of Alvan Clark & Sons.

The Clarks did not make their own raw glass. Pouring huge, flawless disks of optical glass was a specialty of a few glassworks in England and France, and the Clarks bought their blanks there. What they did was the delicate final shaping, called figuring. A large achromatic lens, as you remember from Part 8, is really two lenses, one of crown glass and one of flint glass, working together to cancel out rainbow fringes. Each of their four surfaces must be curved almost perfectly. The Clarks were famous for figuring by hand and eye, rubbing the glass with polishing tools and their own thumbs, testing it on a star, then going back to adjust a tiny spot by a fraction of a wavelength of light.

To test their lenses, the Clarks looked at double stars, pairs so close together that only a very good telescope can split them, and Alvan Clark discovered several new ones himself. In 1862, Alvan Graham Clark was testing a new 18.5-inch lens when he spotted a very faint point of light right next to Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky. Astronomers had predicted from Sirius's wobbling motion that it had a hidden companion. This companion, Sirius B, is a white dwarf, the tiny, super-dense leftover core of a dead star.

Clark lenses soon went into observatories across America and beyond. A 26-inch Clark refractor was installed at the U.S. Naval Observatory in Washington, and in 1877 the astronomer Asaph Hall used it to discover Phobos and Deimos, the two small moons of Mars. Time after time, the Clarks made the largest refracting telescope lens in the world, then beat their own record. Their two greatest lenses, 36 inches and 40 inches across, are the stars of the next section. Today a crater on the Moon and a crater on Mars are named after Alvan Clark.

sections.heading: Monuments on the Mountains: Lick and Yerkes
paragraphs: James Lick was a carpenter and piano maker who became one of the richest men in California by buying land in San Francisco before the city boomed. When he grew old, he wanted to leave something that would make him remembered. He is said to have considered building giant statues or even a pyramid, but friends steered him toward science. In the end he left 700,000 dollars, a huge fortune in the 1870s, to build the most powerful telescope in the world.

The site chosen was the summit of Mount Hamilton, just east of San Jose, at about 1,283 meters (4,209 feet), above much of the valley's haze. To get there, Santa Clara County built a winding road, finished in 1876, that never gets steeper than a 6.5 percent slope, so horse-drawn wagons could haul up heavy parts. It is still in use today as California State Route 130.

Alvan Clark & Sons were asked to make the great lens in 1880; getting flawless glass disks that big from the glassmakers took years and many failed attempts. The finished lens, 36 inches (91 cm) across, arrived in December 1886. James Lick had died in 1876, and in 1887 his body was placed in a tomb inside the foundation of the telescope's pier, the massive column right under the instrument. A brass plaque there says, simply, that here lies the body of James Lick.

The Great Lick Refractor saw first light on 3 January 1888. In May of that year the University of California took over the observatory, and it became the first permanently staffed observatory on a mountaintop anywhere in the world. Astronomers and their families lived on the summit year-round. One of them, the brilliant observer Edward Emerson Barnard, used the 36-inch in 1892 to discover Amalthea, a small moon of Jupiter. It was the first new moon of Jupiter found since Galileo spotted the big four in 1610, almost three centuries earlier.

The Lick refractor's record lasted less than ten years. A young astronomer from Chicago named George Ellery Hale, who would become the greatest telescope builder of the next century, wanted to create an even bigger one. As it happened, Alvan Clark & Sons had two giant 40-inch glass disks on their hands, originally ordered for an observatory planned in Southern California whose money had run out. Hale persuaded Charles Tyson Yerkes, a rich Chicago businessman who ran the city's streetcar lines, to pay for a telescope built around them.

The observatory, run by the University of Chicago, was built at Williams Bay, Wisconsin, on the shore of Lake Geneva. Before installation, the telescope's enormous mounting and tube were shown off at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago. The lens, 40 inches (about 1.02 meters) across, weighs about 225 kilograms, and its focal length is about 19.3 meters. To let astronomers reach the eyepiece, the dome's floor was built as a giant elevator that rose and fell. In 1897, shortly before the opening, the floor's supports broke and it crashed down, luckily when no one was on it.

Yerkes Observatory was dedicated on 21 October 1897. Its 40-inch refractor became, and still is, the largest refracting telescope ever successfully used for astronomy. Albert Einstein toured it in 1921, Edwin Hubble did his graduate work there, and the great astrophysicist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar worked there for many years. The observatory closed in 2018, but a nonprofit group took it over in 2020, and since 2022 visitors can again stand under the great tube, which is being restored.

One important warning: Yerkes is the biggest refractor, not the biggest telescope. As we will see right away, mirror telescopes had already been built much larger, and they would soon leave the lens telescopes far behind.

sections.heading: Why Lenses Stopped Growing
paragraphs: If the 40-inch was so wonderful, why did nobody build a 60-inch or 100-inch lens? People did try to go a little bigger. For the Paris World's Fair of 1900, a giant refractor with a lens about 1.25 meters (49 inches) across was built, with a tube so long it had to lie flat while a big moving mirror fed it light. It was an exhibition wonder, but it was never used for serious research and was taken apart after the fair. The real lesson was clear: lens telescopes had reached their limit, for several reasons.

The first problem is gravity. A lens must let light pass through, so you can only hold it by its edge, like a dinner plate held by its rim. As the telescope tilts, the middle of a big, heavy lens sags very slightly. The sag is far too small to see, but optical surfaces must be accurate to a tiny fraction of a wavelength of light, so a sagging lens blurs the image. Experts reckon the practical limit for a refractor lens is about 1 meter, just the size of the Yerkes lens.

The second problem is the glass itself. All the light must travel through the full thickness of the lens, and glass absorbs some of it, especially the blue and ultraviolet light that old photographic plates were most sensitive to. A few percent more is reflected away at every air-glass surface. Every tiny bubble or streak inside spoils the image, and making a huge, flawless disk of two kinds of glass was so difficult that one failure could cost years. Even then, achromatic lenses still leave a faint purple halo of leftover color, worse in big lenses, and their long tubes need huge, costly domes.

Mirrors avoid almost all of these troubles. Light never passes through a mirror, only bounces off its front surface, so the glass inside does not need to be perfectly clear and its color does not matter. Reflection treats all colors the same, so there is no rainbow fringing at all. Only one surface needs to be shaped perfectly, instead of four. And because nobody needs to see through the back of a mirror, it can be supported from behind across its whole surface, so it does not sag. That is why, after Yerkes, every record-breaking optical telescope has been a reflector.

Great refractors are still treasured for teaching, public viewing and special jobs, but for gathering the faintest light from deep space the future belonged to mirrors. And even the biggest eye forgets what it sees, so astronomers were about to hand the job to something that never blinks: the camera.

deepDive: Two scientific stories in this part are worth a closer look. The first is the Neptune prediction. Le Verrier and Adams both solved what mathematicians call an inverse perturbation problem: instead of starting with planets and computing how they tug on one another, they started from the tugs (the small errors in Uranus's position) and worked backwards to the planet causing them. Both assumed, partly guided by the old Titius-Bode pattern of planetary spacing, that the new planet lay roughly twice as far from the Sun as Saturn, near 38 astronomical units. In fact Neptune orbits at about 30. Their predicted orbits were therefore wrong in size and period, yet the predicted direction in the sky in 1846 was close, because over the few decades of good observations the effect of a closer, lighter planet and a farther, heavier one looked similar. Some historians call this a lucky coincidence of timing; others stress that the method was sound and the direction was the part that mattered for finding it. The credit debate has also shifted. Papers rediscovered in the late 1990s, studied by Nicholas Kollerstrom and others, suggest Adams's predictions varied quite a bit and were not communicated as firm results, which strengthens Le Verrier's priority. The second story is the race between lenses and mirrors, which comes down to numbers. Light grasp scales with area, so the Leviathan's 72-inch mirror had about (72/40)^2, or 3.2 times the area of the Yerkes 40-inch lens. But speculum reflected only roughly 60 to 65 percent of visible light, while a big achromatic lens passes most of the light that enters it, so in practice the gap was smaller than the raw area suggests. The Leviathan also suffered from Irish weather, the stiff limits of its walls, and the difficulty of keeping a 3-ton metal mirror in perfect shape as temperatures changed. The refractors, meanwhile, delivered steady, sharp images, which is why astronomers measuring double stars and planets loved them. What tipped the balance for good was silvered glass, which removed speculum's weakness, plus the fact that a mirror can be supported across its whole back. That opened a path from 60 inches (1908) to 100 inches (1917) to 200 inches (1948), and eventually to the 8- and 10-meter mirrors of today.
funFact: James Lick, who paid for the Lick Observatory, is buried inside the foundation of the 36-inch telescope's pier, so the great refractor has been resting on his tomb since 1887.

check.q: What did Lord Rosse discover when he looked at the nebula M51 through the Leviathan in 1845?
check.a: It had a spiral shape, like a whirlpool
wrong: It was a new planet beyond Uranus
It had a ring like Saturn
It was a comet heading toward Earth
